cards.explanation: The answer is that Jezebel sends him a messenger with a threat. Right after Ahab tells her everything, she sends a messenger to Elijah with these words: “May the gods deal with me, and ever so severely, if by this time tomorrow I have not made your life like the lives of those you killed!” (1 Kings 19:1-2). The message is a threat with a deadline, friends. That is a lot of heat for one delivery.

The answer is True. The text says it plainly: “…Elijah was afraid and ran for his life.” (1 Kings 19:3). This is the prophet who stood on Mount Carmel against Baal's prophets (1 Kings 18:20-40). I think fear can hit hard even after a big moment, friends. The Bible doesn't hide it.

The answer is a day's journey into the wilderness. Elijah leaves his servant in Beersheba, a town in Judah, “…while he himself went a day’s journey into the wilderness.” (1 Kings 19:3-4). Notice he goes out alone. A servant left behind and an empty stretch of wilderness ahead. That is a quiet, lonely picture.

The answer is that he might die. Elijah “…prayed that he might die.” (1 Kings 19:4). His words were, “I have had enough, LORD… Take my life, for I am no better than my fathers.” This is a heavy moment, friends, and I think it hurts to read. Notice that he says it to the LORD, out loud.

The answer is False. There is no servant here, because Elijah left him in Beersheba (1 Kings 19:3). It is an angel who touches Elijah and says, “Get up and eat.” (1 Kings 19:5). Elijah is alone out there, and still someone reaches him.

The answer is bread. There by his head is “…a cake of bread baked over hot coals, and a jar of water.” (1 Kings 19:6). Baked over hot coals, and I respect that, friends. Anything fresh from the heat gets my attention.

The answer is True. “A second time the angel of the LORD returned and touched him…” (1 Kings 19:7). Elijah had already eaten, drunk and lain back down (1 Kings 19:6). So the angel comes back and tells him to get up and eat again. This time the angel adds, “Get up and eat, or the journey will be too much for you.” (1 Kings 19:7).

The answer is that the journey will be too much for him. The angel says, “Get up and eat, or the journey will be too much for you.” (1 Kings 19:7). That is the reason the angel gives, so that is the one we can say, friends. The food is for the journey, and I think it is meant to carry him.

The answer is Horeb. Elijah “…walked forty days and forty nights until he reached Horeb, the mountain of God.” (1 Kings 19:8). Moses, Israel's leader, met God at a burning bush there (Exodus 3:1-4). That is a long walk, friends, and the food gave him strength for it. Forty days is a lot of road.

The answer is that he is the only one left. Elijah says, “I am the only one left, and they are seeking my life as well.” (1 Kings 19:10). That is how he describes his situation to the LORD. I think he feels very alone, friends. Hold on to that line, because it comes back later.

The answer is True. The text says it directly: “…a great and mighty wind tore into the mountains and shattered the rocks before the LORD, but the LORD was not in the wind.” (1 Kings 19:11). That is a LOT of wind, friends, and it is still not Him. A wind that shatters rocks, and the LORD still wasn't in it.

The answer is False. “After the earthquake there was a fire, but the LORD was not in the fire.” (1 Kings 19:12). The wind and the earthquake came first, and He wasn't in those either. That is the third big thing in a row, and none of them was Him. I've been near plenty of ovens, friends, so I can tell you fire gets all the attention.

The answer is a still small voice. “…after the fire came a still, small voice.” (1 Kings 19:12). After all that noise, it is quiet. I love that the text lets the quiet land, friends. Wind, earthquake, fire, and then a whisper of a sound.

The answer is that he wraps his face in his cloak and steps out. “When Elijah heard it, he wrapped his face in his cloak and went out and stood at the mouth of the cave.” (1 Kings 19:13). He doesn't stay hidden, friends. He covers his face, and still goes out to stand there. That says a lot about how he took in that voice.

The answer is that he says the same thing he said the first time. Elijah answers with the same words: “I have been very zealous for the LORD, the God of Hosts… I am the only one left, and they are seeking my life as well” (1 Kings 19:14). They match what he said in verse 10. The text doesn't say why he repeats it, so I won't guess too hard, friends. I will say the answer comes out word for word.

The answer is prophet in Elijah's place. The LORD says to anoint “…Elisha son of Shaphat from Abel-meholah to succeed you as prophet.” (1 Kings 19:16). So Elisha, a man from Abel-meholah, is the one set to take over as prophet. The work is meant to go on past Elijah, friends. I like that the LORD has a plan for what comes next.

The answer is False. The LORD says, “…I have reserved seven thousand in Israel…” and those are the ones whose knees have not bowed to Baal (1 Kings 19:18). Elijah had said, “I am the only one left…” (1 Kings 19:14). Seven thousand is quite a number for one lonely prophet, friends.

The answer is cloak. “Elijah passed by him and threw his cloak around him.” (1 Kings 19:19). The cloak is the thing the text gives, friends. Elijah passes by, and the cloak goes around Elisha. That is a bold way to make an introduction.

The answer is to kiss his father and mother goodbye. Elisha says, “Please let me kiss my father and mother goodbye, and then I will follow you.” (1 Kings 19:20). That is his one request, friends. Elijah answers, “Go on back…” and asks, “for what have I done to you?” Elisha asks to say goodbye first, and he says he will follow.

The answer is that he slaughters them and feeds the people. Elisha “…took his pair of oxen, and slaughtered them.” and then “…cooked the meat and gave it to the people, and they ate.” (1 Kings 19:21). The oxen were the team he was plowing with (1 Kings 19:19), and he gives the meat to the people. I think that is a big way to head out the door, friends.

The answer is True. “Then he set out to follow and serve Elijah.” (1 Kings 19:21). Elisha had cooked the meat and given it to the people, and they ate. After that, Elisha goes after Elijah. Elijah, the man who ran, now has someone who set out to follow and serve him.
